reason: The top-ranked candidate at 7:2 and at 7:4, on a six-word run, and it is the King James Bible's genealogical boilerplate. “he begat sons and daughters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, but the phrase without the pronoun occurs in eighteen, and every one of them is Genesis 5 or Genesis 11 — the antediluvian and post-Babel descent lists. That is a formula, not a source: the KJV writes it once per generation for sixteen generations precisely because it carries no information. The Book of Mormon uses it the same way, four times in this chapter alone (7:2, 7:4, 7:12, 7:26), and it enters Ether earlier still, at 6:15-16, so 7:2 is not even its first Jaredite occurrence. The second machine proposal here, 2 Chronicles 24:3 (Jehoiada's two wives), is the same string in a narrative with nothing else in common. Numbers 26:62 was also proposed, for 'twenty and three', which in that verse is a Levite census figure in thousands. What Ether 7:1-2 does with its numbers is argued at the Judges 10:4 link on this verse; the begetting formula is not part of that argument.

The machine's only candidate at 7:3, and it is the right chapter of the Bible for the wrong reason. Genesis 37:3 reads 'because he was the son of his old age', and “son of his old age” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — a genuine rarity, but a different construction from the one Ether has. The Book of Mormon's string is 'begat Kib in his old age', and “in his old age” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 21:2 and Genesis 21:7, both of them Isaac's birth to Abraham. The link is written at this verse to Genesis 21:2, and the Isaac context is what makes it worth writing; Joseph's coat contributes nothing.

A four-word run and a real temptation, because both verses are about a son set against his father and a household divided. The senses are opposed at the only point that matters. Matthew 10:35 is Christ describing the cost of discipleship — the division is caused by the gospel, the divided son is in the right, and the saying is a warning issued by the one who causes it. Ether 7:4 is a prince of thirty-two raising an army to depose his father and put him in captivity, an act the chapter treats as the first crime in Jaredite history and the fulfilment of a prophecy of bondage. Matthew's variance is a consequence of righteousness; Corihor's is rebellion. Nothing else of Matthew 10 is present, and the daughters and mothers-in-law that make up the rest of the verse have no counterpart. The real borrowing in this verse is at its other end — 'drew away many people after him', Acts 5:37 — and is catalogued as a link.

This entry has to be written because the count is seductive and wrong. “in the stead of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 22:13, where Abraham offers the ram 'for a burnt offering in the stead of his son' — and Ether 7 is a chapter about fathers, sons, and one son taking a father's place. A reader who runs the phrase will find a singleton attached to the Bible's central substitution scene and will be tempted to catalogue it. The rarity is arithmetic, in exactly the way the register's Helaman 1:1 entry describes. 'In his stead' and 'in the stead of' are among the KJV's commonest constructions — “reigned in his stead” alone occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses — and the string here is long only because 'his father' happens to follow, as 'his son' happens to follow in Genesis 22:13. The two verses share a preposition and a possessive. Ether 7:10 is a succession notice; Genesis 22:13 is a sacrifice. The succession formula itself is adjudicated at 7:3.

The highest-scoring candidate at 7:10, and it is the regnal accession formula, which the KJV uses of nearly every king of Israel and Judah. Shallum the son of Jabesh contributes nothing but the syntax of beginning to reign; his month in Samaria has no counterpart here. The Book of Mormon's use of the KJV's dynastic formulary is a real feature of this chapter and is adjudicated as a structural link at 7:3, to the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31-39, on the grounds that no single one of the sixty-three 'reigned in his stead' verses can be named as a source. This candidate is superseded by that row.

A six-word run, the top candidate at 7:11, and the sense is inverted. Ezekiel 34:6 is the indictment of the shepherds of Israel: 'my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek after them.' The phrase there measures a catastrophe of dispersal caused by rulers who failed. Ether 7:11 reads 'he did spread his kingdom upon all the face of the land, for the people had become exceeding numerous' — the same words measuring a good king's dominion over a growing people. Scattering against spreading, abandonment against government, earth against land. The Book of Mormon uses 'upon all the face of the earth' in the Ezekiel sense elsewhere and it is covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; what is recorded here is that its appearance at 7:11 is the opposite sense and is not a borrowing from Ezekiel. The verse's real KJV contact is 'did execute judgement in righteousness', which is adjudicated at 7:1 with this verse in recurrenceRefs.

Recorded because a reader will notice it and should be told the catalogue noticed too. Ether 7 names two Jaredite princes after figures of Genesis 1-11 — Noah at 7:14 and Nimrod at 7:22 — in a book whose founding event is the confounding of tongues at Babel. The Nimrod case is catalogued as a link at 7:22, because Genesis 10:10 attaches a kingdom to that name and Ether 7:22 has this Nimrod dispose of one, so the borrowing does argumentative work. The Noah case will not carry the same weight. There is no shared wording of any kind: Ether 7:14-18 gives its Noah a rebellion, a battle, a captive king and a murder in the night, and Genesis gives its Noah an ark, and the only point of contact is four letters. Worse, the sense runs backwards — the KJV's Noah is the one just man in a generation of violence, and Ether's is the usurper who takes a king captive and is killed in his own house. The Book of Mormon's other wicked King Noah, at Mosiah 11, raises the same question, and it is a question for that book rather than this one. Filed here at insufficient-verbal rather than wrong-sense because there is no verbal contact to have a sense at all.

A genuine KJV singleton — “carried him away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the sequence is close: the chief priests bind Jesus, carry him away, deliver him to Pilate, and he is put to death; Noah takes Shule the king, carries him away captive, and is about to put him to death. It is displaced rather than rejected. Jeremiah 52:9 accounts for the whole of Ether's clause and not three words of it: “took the king and carried” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Ether 7:17 has the object ('the king'), the verb pair, the qualifier 'captive' and a named destination, which is the Babylonian deportation formula entire. Mark 15:1 has no 'king', no 'captive' and no destination. The link is written at this verse to Jeremiah 52:9 with Mark 15:1 named in its provenance, so a reader who finds the singleton is not left thinking it went unseen.

The top candidate at 7:18 on a five-word run, and it is pure syntax. Acts 20:3 has Paul 'about to sail into Syria' when the Jews lay wait for him; Ether 7:18 has Noah 'about to put him to death' when the sons of Shule break into his house. The construction marks an interrupted intention, which is the commonest possible narrative use for it, and the two intentions have nothing in common. Nothing else of Acts 20 is present.

This is the entry the Judges 3:26 Ehud case in Helaman is the model for: the typology pulls hard and the wording will not bear it. Ether 7:18 is a night rescue from prison on the eve of an execution — Noah is 'about to put him to death', the sons of Shule enter the house by night, kill him, break down the door of the prison and bring their father out — and the King James Bible has one famous scene of that shape, Acts 12: Herod means to bring Peter forth after Easter, the angel comes 'the same night', the chains fall off and the iron gate opens of its own accord. The shared elements are the eve of execution, the night, the door and the deliverance. There is not one shared distinctive word, and the difference is doctrinal rather than incidental: Acts 12's whole point is that no human agency is involved, the keepers are asleep and the gate opens by itself, whereas Ether's deliverance is a homicide and a broken door. A second candidate has to be recorded with it. 2 Kings 11 has the usurper who holds a throne against its rightful occupant slain by a counter-coup and the true king enthroned — Athaliah killed, Joash crowned — which is Ether 7:18-19's plot exactly, and 2 Kings 11:17 was in fact proposed by the machine at 7:19 on 'the king and the people'. It likewise has no verbal contact: Ether shares with 2 Kings 11 no phrase longer than the definite article. Both are recorded here so that a reader who sees either type is told the catalogue saw it and declined to catalogue it as dependence. Either would become a link if a distinctive phrase were found; neither has one.

A five-word run consisting of two nouns and three articles. 2 Kings 11:17 is Jehoiada's covenant between the LORD, the king and the people; Ether 7:19 is a note that the people under Shule's reign prospered. The pairing of a king with his people is not a phrase anyone borrows. The chapter's real relation to 2 Kings 11 — the usurper slain, the rightful king restored — is discussed in the exclusion at 7:18, where it is declined for want of verbal contact.

Worth an entry only because of what the spelling shows. “favour in the eyes of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:25 — David, fleeing Absalom's rebellion, sending the ark back with Zadok, 'if I shall find favour in the eyes of the LORD' — and Ether 7:22 reads 'he did gain favor in the eyes of Shule', in a chapter that is itself a chain of rebellions against a father. The singleton is arithmetic all the same: the KJV's ordinary idioms are 'found grace in the eyes of' and 'found favour in the sight of', which between them run to dozens of verses, and the one occurrence of this variant is an accident of which noun and which preposition happened to meet. The verb is wrong as well — the KJV never 'gains' favour, it finds it. The negative datum is the useful part: the 1830 spells the word 'favor', not the KJV's 'favour', and CONVENTIONS §8 cuts both ways. Where 1830 keeps a KJV spelling that is evidence of copying; where it does not, as here, it is evidence that this phrase was not being copied from a King James page.

The best entry in this chapter's register and the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter. “which gave power unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “gave power unto”: Revelation 13:4, 'they worshipped the dragon which gave power unto the beast'. Ether 7:25 reads 'he did execute a law throughout all the land, which gave power unto the prophets that they should go whithersoever they would'. Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton is normally decisive evidence in this catalogue, and here it is worthless, because the two sentences are opposites at every joint. In Revelation the giver is the dragon, the receiver is the beast, and what is conferred is the authority to make war on the saints and to be worshipped in God's place; the verse is the KJV's compressed statement of illegitimate power. In Ether the giver is a king acting by law, the receivers are prophets, and what is conferred is nothing but freedom of movement — the right to go where they will and say what they were sent to say. Revelation's clause describes a delegation of tyranny; Ether's describes a statute protecting speech. The grammatical coincidence is complete and the sense is inverted, which is precisely the shape CONVENTIONS §5 asks to be written up at length rather than passed over: a reader who runs the phrase will find the singleton, and must be told that the catalogue found it first and rejected it.

Proposed at 7:27 for a four-word run, and the run is the whole of it. 2 Kings 8:4 is Gehazi telling the king of Israel 'all the great things that Elisha hath done' — a servant entertaining a court with prophet anecdotes. Ether 7:27 has Shule remembering 'the great things that the Lord had done for his fathers in bringing them across the great deep into the promised land': the agent is God and not a prophet, the beneficiaries are the ancestors and not the hearer, and the content is a founding deliverance. The verse's contacts are catalogued as a link to Judges 2:7, whose 'great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel' supplies the thought, with 1 Kings 8:66 in composite for the exact run “the Lord had done for”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
